platforms.title: Chronic Fatigue: 3 Everyday Habits That Quietly Drain Your Energy
platforms.meta_description: Chronic fatigue isn't always about sleep. Mild dehydration, low magnesium, and late-night screen time can quietly drain your energy every day.
platforms.body_html:
When exhaustion lingers no matter how many hours you sleep, it's tempting to assume the problem is the sleep itself. But at least three ordinary daily habits can quietly drain energy regardless of how much time you spend in bed: running low on water, falling short on magnesium, and scrolling on a bright phone before sleep. Here's how each one plays a role, and what actually helps.

Mild Dehydration and Fatigue

Losing as little as 1.5% of body weight in fluid counts as mild dehydration, and research from the University of Connecticut found it was enough to worsen mood, raise perceived fatigue, and dull concentration in both men and women — often before anyone even felt thirsty. Coffee and soda don't rehydrate the way plain water does, since caffeine has a mild diuretic effect that can offset some of the fluid gained. Most adults reach this level of mild dehydration at least once a week without realizing it.

Falling Short on Magnesium

According to National Institutes of Health data, nearly half of American adults take in less magnesium through food than recommended, with an estimated 15% deficient enough to affect health. Magnesium is directly involved in energy metabolism, helping cells convert food into usable energy — running low leaves that process short-changed throughout the day, on top of effects on muscle function and sleep quality. Spinach, almonds, and pumpkin seeds are among the most accessible everyday sources.

Screen Time Before Bed

Blue light from phones and other backlit screens suppresses melatonin, the hormone that signals it's time to sleep. Research on light exposure before bedtime has found melatonin suppression ranging from roughly 23% after one hour to as much as 38-46% after two hours of screen exposure, depending on the study population. Less melatonin means it takes longer to fall asleep and less time is spent in deep, restorative sleep stages — even after a full eight hours in bed, that sleep ends up lower quality.

What Actually Helps

  • Carry a water bottle — Sipping throughout the day, before thirst sets in, helps avoid the dip in mood and focus that mild dehydration causes.
  • Add magnesium-rich foods to a meal — Spinach, almonds, or pumpkin seeds are simple, accessible ways to close the gap.
  • Put the phone down an hour before bed — Dimming lights and switching to a book or a low-light routine protects melatonin release.

The Bottom Line

None of these three habits need to be eliminated completely — small, consistent changes to water intake, meals, and evening screen use can meaningfully lighten how heavy tomorrow feels. This article is for general information only and isn't medical advice. If fatigue continues for more than two weeks despite adequate sleep, it's worth checking in with a doctor to rule out other causes.
